claims.text: A compound-index prefix consists of consecutive fields starting at the first index field. A sort matching such a prefix can use its ordering; a filter using the index does not by itself establish sort compatibility. (high confidence)

A non-prefix sort subset can use index order when all preceding index fields have equality predicates. With {a:1,b:1,c:1}, find({a:5}).sort({b:1,c:1}) qualifies; omitting equality on a generally prevents that suffix from supplying global order through one scan. (high confidence)

When an equality predicate fixes the leading field, a single remaining sort field can use either scan direction. For {type:1,timestamp:1}, find({type:"click"}).sort({timestamp:-1}) can use the same index as the ascending timestamp query. (high confidence)

Use explain to distinguish index access from order provision: IXSCAN identifies index access, while an explicit SORT indicates additional sorting. Merely seeing an index scan is insufficient evidence that the index supplies the requested order. (medium confidence)

For an unconstrained compound sort, sort fields must occur in index field order. An index {a:1,b:-1} can provide {a:1,b:-1} or {a:-1,b:1}, but cannot provide {a:1,b:1}, {a:-1,b:-1}, or the reordered sort {b:-1,a:1}. (high confidence)

For sort preservation, equality fields generally precede sort fields, and range fields follow them. A highly selective range can instead justify ERS and a subsequent blocking sort, so ESR is a guideline rather than a guarantee of the fastest plan. (medium confidence)
A compound index orders entries lexicographically by its declared field sequence. Field order therefore affects which query and sort patterns it can serve efficiently. (high confidence)
A leading index prefix can supply sort order without equality predicates on those sort fields; for example, {a:1,b:1,c:1,d:1} supports sorting by {a:1,b:1} or {a:-1,b:-1}. (high confidence)

A range predicate does not universally prevent index-provided sorting. With {a:1,b:1,c:1,d:1}, find({a:{$gt:4}}).sort({a:1,b:1}) preserves index order; a range on an omitted preceding field does not generally provide global order for a later sort field. (high confidence)

Small $in lists used with sort can be expanded into equality-like scans whose outputs are combined by SORT_MERGE; this does not remove the need for compatible suffix sort fields and directions. Larger lists can behave like ranges, preventing later index fields from providing sort order. (medium confidence)

SERVER-14070 records a historical planner defect where {a:1,b:1} and find({a:1,b:1}).sort({b:1}) unnecessarily required sorting. The issue lists fixes in 2.6.11 and 2.8.0-rc3; this is historical evidence, not a claim that modern versions retain the bug. (low confidence)

A range predicate does not universally disqualify index-provided sorting. For {a:1,b:1}, find({a:{$gt:4}}).sort({a:1,b:1}) retains index order; the difficulty is skipping a varying preceding key while sorting a later key alone. (high confidence)

Inference for SORT_MERGE: equality expansion can expose ordered suffix streams, but it does not remove the suffix field-order and direction requirements. Qualify each branch against those requirements before attributing a missing blocking sort to an ordered merge. (medium confidence)
